cells.tense: You stand in the engine room and the machines run because you stay near them.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Start the thing you keep circling — one step, before the route is clear. Wanting it counts as reason enough. How it ends isn't the part you need in order to begin.
cells.core:
Under a load, you keep one thing warm without burning down. You hold steady, the people working beside you catch their second wind from it, and you don't need to see how it finishes to keep it going. What you do well is tend what keeps the work moving.

And something has been circling in you for a while. Begin it this week, before you can see the whole way — no route drawn, no certainty bought, wanting it counting as the reason. How it turns out stays unclear longer than you'd choose, and somebody will ask where you're headed before you can say. Fine. The first step settles the direction, and the road shows up under your feet.

cells.tense: You are packing for a crossing you have decided is coming, and carrying what isn't needed yet.
cells.act: say the hard thing gently, once
cells.ask: When you next move a plan with someone, give them the piece they can use now, not the whole arc or the case for it. Say it plainly once. The rest waits until they've caught up.
cells.core:
Under pressure you keep the fire so far in front of this moment that the present has nobody in it. You're bracing for what hasn't happened, pushing the warmth toward a version of things that isn't here, and the people you're keeping going get hurried past. The strength is real. It's aimed at a crossing that may not come this way.

Watch what actually lands when you talk. Next time you move something forward with someone, hand them the single piece they need next — not the whole shape of where it ends. Say that much, once, and stop there. That brings the fire back to where the feet are. Some of the forward lean is what keeps things moving; keep it. What changes is how far in front of them you stand when you speak.

cells.tense: The fire is behind you, and you are standing at a door you already walked through.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Something near you is finished — a job, a role, a pile of stuff. This week, close it for good: hand it off, empty the shelf, finish the last piece. Keep only what still serves what comes next.
cells.core:
The room is quiet and you keep checking the gauge. The strength you're known for has nothing on it — you're keeping a fire with no pot over it, and what you can bear isn't getting spent on anything real. So when something genuinely heavy arrives, you slip out from under it, not trusting what you can hold.

Within arm's reach, something is over. Close it this week. Hand it off, empty the shelf, finish the last piece. Nothing more than that ending. When the done thing leaves, the surface beneath it shows what was holding, and the warmth has somewhere to go again.

cells.tense: You keep the fire going and call it luck; someone else gets the credit for it.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Take whatever you keep steadiest and give it one real inch of work: the next small piece, done slowly by hand, with the finished result left where it stands.
cells.core:
You can hold steady and keep people warm without ever putting your name on the cause. The picking, the coaxing, the second wind the others catch — it happens because of you, and you file it under the situation, or say you were only going along with what was needed. The warmth gets through to them. Your part in it doesn't.

Whatever you keep steadiest, move it one real inch this week. Do the work slowly by hand, and leave the result where it stands — no explaining, no taking it back. That inch is the whole correction: the fire you keep has a maker, and the next time you tend one, you'll feel your own weight in it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the balanced cell's tending is 'freely' chosen — the record supports kept-steady and warm, not that the cost doesn't bite. A reader could reasonably say I'm describing someone who never tires, when the mechanism is exactly tending-without-burning-out, which implies it can. The ask survives being wrong: if the read misses, they still tested one support in a week that will have stress in it either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You are the one who keeps the fire lit' — it congratulates the pattern instead of handing it over, so it goes. Too Much and Too Little are written as opposite failures: throwing energy past the person versus refusing to spend any, one holding nothing steady, one holding everything still.
